big: A conglomerate has telecom, retail and energy arms. One P/E cannot describe all three. Different businesses call for different tools: sum of the parts, assets, dividends or comparison with peers.

lines: Is DCF enough for every company?

No. A conglomerate is valued arm by arm. A land-rich firm is valued on its plots less its loans. A mature utility is valued on its steady dividends. A paint maker is judged against other listed paint makers.

rows: plots at market value less loans

q: A conglomerate with telecom, retail and energy arms is valued arm by arm. What is this?
why: Asset-based uses what a company owns less owes.
Each business is valued separately and added.
A DDM uses dividends. It does not fit the facts given.

q: A land-rich firm is valued on its plots at market value less its loans. What is this?
why: It is based on what is owned minus what is owed.
Sum of the parts splits by business. It does not fit the facts given.
Relative valuation uses peers. It does not fit the facts given.
A margin of safety is a gap. It does not answer what was asked.

q: A mature utility pays steady payouts. Which model values it on those payouts?
why: Sum of the parts splits by business. That does not match this case.
It values a share as the present value of expected dividends.
Asset-based looks at owned assets. It does not answer what was asked.
Scenario analysis tests stories. The details here point elsewhere.

q: A paint maker is judged against other listed paint makers. What is this?
why: Sum of the parts splits by arm. It does not fit the facts given.
Asset-based uses net assets. It does not answer what was asked.
A DDM uses dividends. The details here point elsewhere.
It compares a company with similar companies.

pts: Sum of the parts: value each business, then add.
Asset-based: assets minus liabilities. DDM: present value of dividends.
Relative valuation: compare with similar companies.
